newsitem.title: ROMANIA: ROMANIA'S INTERNAL PUBLIC DEBT SOARS IN 1996.
newsitem.headline: ROMANIA'S INTERNAL PUBLIC DEBT SOARS IN 1996.

text.p: Romania's internal public debt rose to 6.69 trillion lei ($976.6 million) at the end of last year from 2.8 trillion at end-1995, a Finance Ministry report said on Friday.
It said the bulk of the 1996 debt growth was a result of funding or refinancing of state budget deficits over the past three years.

Economists said the internal public debt had risen mainly in the second half of 1996, when the former ruling leftists "turned the tap on spending" ahead of elections, held last November. The budget gap was covered through several issues of leu- or dollar-denominated treasury bills.

With most papers having 90-day maturity, the new centrist coalition government had to issued several rollover bills in the past three months. Only in March the Finance Ministry launched around 900 billion lei in floating rate T-bills.

The bills offer attractive returns -- calculated at the average of the auctioned rates on the central bank's one-week funds -- but local bankers said their current yield was "burdening" for the budget.

In a bid to fight soaring inflation, Romania's tough monetary policies have pushed the auctioned rate to an all-time peak of 426.5 percent last month from 50 percent in the New Year. Despite its recent fall, bankers say the rate, running now at 220.02 percent, is still "expensive for the budget".
Last week, the new government approved the draft of the 1997 state budget, with public debt spendings at 9.79 trillion lei, or about 18 percent of total expenditure.
The bill, a plank for new loans from the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, put the 1997 state budget gap at 5.4 percent of the gross domestic product.

It also set a lower consolidated budget deficit, at 4.5 percent of GDP against 5.8 last year. Parliament, where the ruling coalition has a comfortable majority, is expected to endorse the draft within one month.
The bulk of the 1997 gap will be financed through external loans -- about 3.4 percent -- with the rest funded by domestic credits. -- Mirela Eremia, Bucharest Newsroom 40-1 3120264
